newsitem.title: BOSNIA: ATHLETICS-TIMES COME SECOND AS SPORT RETURNS TO SARAJEVO.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-TIMES COME SECOND AS SPORT RETURNS TO SARAJEVO.

text.p: For once results were of secondary importance when world class athletics returned to Sarajevo for the first time in four years on a memorable day in this Bosnian capital on Monday.
"The heart of our city is beating again," said Enver Jiga, one of the organisers of the International Amateur Athletic Federation's Solidarity Meeting and the re-opening of Kosevo Stadium.

The meeting, featuring 80 athletes from 30 countries including five Atlanta Olympic champions, was the biggest international event held in Sarajevo since the end of the war which followed the break-up of the former Yugoslavia.
While the results and performances were second in importance to the fact the event was taking place at all, there were several impressive races on the newly laid track.

John Mayock of Britain, a journeyman middle-distance runner who risked losing his job as a sports development officer to compete, scored the biggest win of his career in the 2,000 metres when he beat new world 2,000 metre record-holder Salah Hissou of Morocco. Mayock clocked five minutes 00.91 seconds, 4/100ths of a second faster than the north African.

The 50,000 capacity crowd was also treated to a superb race in the women's 1,500 metres when Carla Sacramento of Portugal pipped the 44-year-old evergeen Russian Yekaterina Podkopayeva in a thrilling finish.

There were also wins for Olympic champions Ludmilla Enquist of Sweden in the women's 100 metres hurdles, Balasz Kiss of Hungary in the hammer throw and American Charles Austin in the high jump, but almost every performance was greeted by cheers by the sport-starved crowd.
Bosnia-Herzogevina President Alija Izetbegovic officially opened the meeting being staged in the stadium where the opening and closing cermonies of the 1984 Winter Olympics were held.

Two dozen white doves, symbolising renewed peace and hope, were released at the conclusion of his speech which followed a welcome by Primo Nebiolo, president of the IAAF and a prime mover in organising the meeting.
"Sarajevo, welcome back to world athletics, welcome back to the world of sport," Nebiolo said to rapturous applause.

Images of the lighting of the torch for the 1984 Games were flashed on a videoscreen shipped in for the occasion. The same Olympic tower stands starkly today, blackened by the shells that rained on the stadium during the war as artillery fire blasted the city.
The IAAF and the IOC contributed $1.5 million towards rebuilding the stadium, including new seating, a newly laid football pitch and the athletics track.
Nebiolo earlier made another attack on leading athletes who had refused to attend the meeting, accusing them of lacking bravery.
"One great athlete told me yesterday he did not want to come because of the situation in Serbia. I had to explain to him that Bosnia was not Serbia and that it was not in Africa.

"Another great champion told me he did not want to come because he might get shot, I told him: `I am Primo Nebiolo, I am more important than you, do you think they would want to shoot you when they could shoot me instead'."
